en: The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching to Mahākāśyapa Regarding the Deliverance of the Poor Mother, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of Khotan during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, having delivered its rulers and people, together with his retinue...
A vast assembly—consisting of the destitute, bodhisattva mahāsattvas, devas, nāgas, spirits, and countless people of the world—gathered to hear the sutra.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa traveled alone on a mission of conversion and arrived at the city of Rājagṛha; constantly practicing great compassion and bestowing blessings upon sentient beings, he renounced the wealthy and noble to beg from the poor.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa desired to go on his alms-round, thinking:
"If I am to set out, I should first enter into samādhi; what poor person might I then bring to merit?"

He immediately entered the great city of Rājagṛha and saw a solitary mother in extreme poverty, who, amidst a great heap of filth in the streets and alleys, had dug a cave-like hollow into the side of that heap. Emaciated and afflicted by illness, she lay constantly within it; alone and destitute, possessing neither food nor clothing, she had merely erected a small fence around the cave to shield her body from view.
Through the Kāśyapa-samādhi, he knew that this person had not planted roots of merit in past lives, which was why he was poor now; he also knew that his mother’s life span would end soon:
"If I do not deliver her, she will forever lose the hall of blessings."

At that time, the mother was suffering from hunger and exhaustion; the householder’s maidservant discarded some rice-water that was foul and indescribable. The mother begged for it, and the woman immediately placed it in a broken tile shard beside her.
Mahākāśyapa went to her place and made this prayer:
"Give me even a small amount; you shall obtain great merit.
At that time, the old woman spoke these verses:
"With my entire body afflicted by disease, how can my solitary poverty even be described?
The poorest in the whole land, with food and clothing barely covering my form—
even those in this world who lack compassion still look upon me with pity and sympathy."
What is called compassion? Why do you not know of this calamity?
The cold and suffering of the entire world does not exceed that of my own body;
I pray for your pity and forgiveness, for it is truly not out of a desire for personal virtue that I speak.
Mahākāśyapa then replied with a verse:
"The Buddha is the Honored One of the three realms, and I am fully included therein;
wishing to remove your hunger and poverty, I therefore beg from you who are poor."
"If one can diminish what pertains to body and speech, And give even a fraction of a grain as an offering,
One will attain liberation through the long night, And in future births,
attain great wealth. At that time, the old woman spoke again in verse:
"Truly as you have said, having been born into this world without merit, I now dwell within a pit of dung, my body smeared with impurities.
For food I have no portion of rice; my emaciated form is left uncovered."
"Now, being extremely poor, my intention to give is thwarted by my circumstances.
Mahākāśyapa spoke again in verse:
"The mother speaks of a place she does not find pleasing; starving and destitute, there is nothing with which to give."
If one possesses the intention to give, one will not be poor;
if, moreover, one knows shame and modesty, one is truly clad in the Dharma-robes.
These two qualities, like a mother, ensure that one's food and clothing are fully provided.
In this world there are foolish people who, though possessing abundant clothing, jewels, and grain, are shameless and do not think of giving;
they will be reckoned as great paupers in the future.
To establish merit and virtue amidst such desolation may truly be called rare.
"Truly, the multitude of sins and blessings—sincerity does not speak falsely.

At that time, the old woman heard the verse and was filled with joy; she thought to herself that she had some foul rice-water from the previous day which she could not bear to drink, so she called out to Kāśyapa from afar:
"Have pity on me; will you accept it?"
Mahākāśyapa replied, "Very well!

The mother then crawled on her hands and knees inside the cave to retrieve it; as her body was naked and she could not carry it out, she turned sideways with a hunched back and handed it over from atop the fence.
Kāśyapa accepted it, and the Honored One recited a blessing:
"May you receive blessings and peace.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"If I were to take this away and drink it elsewhere, my mother would not believe me and would say that I have discarded it.
He then drank it all before his mother, rinsed the bowl, and returned it to the cloth bag.
Thereupon, the old woman’s genuine faith was restored.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"I must manifest my supernormal powers so that this woman may surely attain great peace."
He immediately sank into the earth and then appeared again in the void, emitting water and fire from his body:
from the upper half of his body water issued forth, while from the lower half fire issued forth.
Furthermore, he manifested transformations and altered his appearance, soaring through the void; he emerged from the east and vanished in the west, and likewise in the south and north.
At that time, the woman, seeing this, leaped for joy and knelt single-mindedly, gazing afar at Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa said:

"Mother, what is it that you now desire in your heart? Is it the wealth and nobility of the world, the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, or the rank of the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, or Brahmā among the various devas?"
Furthermore, if one wishes to attain the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or pratyekabuddha;
or if one wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, that is, the state of an avaivartika Buddha—[one should practice this samādhi].
"You shall all attain the fruits of your vows.

At that time, the woman grew weary of the sufferings of the world; having heard that the heavens above were truly a place of bliss, she addressed Kāśyapa, saying, "I pray that by this small merit I may be reborn in the heavens."
Thereupon, Kāśyapa suddenly vanished.

After several days, the old woman’s life came to an end, and she was immediately reborn in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Her majestic virtue was so towering that it shook heaven and earth; her radiance was so preeminent that it was like seven suns rising at once to illuminate the celestial palace.
Śakra Devānām Indra was immediately seized with alarm and trepidation, thinking:
"What person possesses such merit as to move [the heavens] in this way? Could there not be someone here who surpasses me?
He then observed with his divine eye and saw that it was the merit of this goddess that had caused it to happen.
Śakra Devānām-Indra then asked in verse:
"From where has this woman come?
A great radiance shines forth, like seven suns appearing all at once."
"This palace of mine trembles; its majestic power is difficult to withstand.
What merit did I originally cultivate to come and ascend to this heaven?
At that time, the goddess answered Śakra with a verse:
"Originally in Jambudvīpa, within an impure den of excrement,
Wasted by age and beset by illness, lacking sufficient food and clothing.
In the trichiliocosm, the Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha— ”
Next was a great disciple named Mahākāśyapa.
Moved by compassion, he begged from his maternal aunt; when she heard him preach the Dharma, her heart rejoiced.
She offered him a gift of fermented rice-water; though her offering was small, the merit she gained was vast.
"With a single mind making offerings at this field of merit, and wishing to be born in the heavens,
though casting off this body within a pit of filth, one shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, the goddess thought to herself:

"This meritorious retribution is due to his having made offerings to Kāśyapa in a previous life; even if one were to bestow upon Kāśyapa hundreds of thousands of various kinds of celestial treasures, it would still not repay even a moment's worth of his kindness."

Immediately, a maidservant carrying celestial incense and flowers descended suddenly; she scattered them over Kāśyapa from mid-air, and then descended herself, prostrating with her five limbs touching the ground.
Having completed the rites, he withdrew and stood with palms joined, sighing and saying:
"In the great trichiliocosm, the Buddha is uniquely most honored; next is Kāśyapa, who is able to close the gates of transgression."
Long ago, while at a dung-pit in Jambudvīpa, he expounded the True Words for the sake of his poor mother.
At that time, the mother rejoiced and offered him a handful of rice; though her gift was as small as a mustard seed, she obtained a reward as vast as a mountain.
"Having attained the state of a celestial maiden and received the natural endowment,
she has therefore descended here to take refuge in the Field of Merit.
Having spoken thus, the celestial maiden, together with her attendants, immediately returned to the heavens.
Thereupon, Śakra thought to himself:

"This woman, amidst the foul and impure conditions of Jambudvīpa, has offered this gruel to Kāśyapa and thereby attained such merit. Kāśyapa possesses great compassion, yet the merit of those from inferior families cannot equal that of those from great clans."
"You should devise an excellent plan: go to the place where Kāśyapa is in Jambudvīpa and establish meritorious blessings.

Śakra-devendra then took the Queen and, carrying food of a hundred flavors in small jars, went down to the side of a lane in the great city of Rājagṛha and built a small, humble hut. He transformed his appearance to resemble an old man, with a body emaciated by illness, walking with a stoop; he and his wife wove mats together, manifesting the guise of poor beggars, without storing any provisions of food, grain, or silk.
Later, as Mahākāśyapa was walking for alms, he saw this poor man and went to him to beg for food.
The man said, "I am so impoverished that I have nothing; what can I do?"
Kāśyapa offered prayers of blessing and remained there for a long while without departing.
The man said, "We, husband and wife, are very old; we have no leisure even to weave mats. We were just now begging for a little rice, intending to eat it as soon as we received it."
Having heard of your benevolent virtue, I have come from poverty to beg for the sake of merit.
Although I am currently destitute, my mind is resolved to sacrifice and give to you, a worthy man; if it is indeed as you say, may I thereby obtain merit.

The fragrance of the celestial food was such as had never been heard of in the world; when the jar was opened in advance, its exquisite scent wafted forth, and Kāśyapa, perceiving it, was utterly unwilling to accept it.
He then said, "O practitioner!..."
"The food is meager; please take it in your bowl.
Kāśyapa took it in his bowl and offered the prayer of blessing:
"May the fragrance of this offering pervade the great city of Rājagṛha and its entire realm."

Kāśyapa was immediately struck by the immeasurable fragrance; he then entered samādhi to contemplate its origin. Just as he sat in samādhi, the man and his mother returned to their original forms as Śākya devas and flew away swiftly, snapping their fingers in the air with immeasurable joy.
Kāśyapa reflected and immediately knew that Śakra had transformed himself into an old man to manifest this change in order to increase his merit and fortune.
He thought, "I have now accepted it; it is not appropriate for me to return it."
Kāśyapa praised him, saying, "Excellent, Śakra!
Never weary of planting merit, you have endured this ignoble form to descend and cultivate merit; you shall surely obtain its corresponding reward."
Śakra and his queen were all the more filled with joy and exultation.
At that time, celestial music came to welcome them, and upon arriving at the palace, Śakra’s delight increased even further.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"This poor woman is one whom no one in all the world can equal; though her gift was meager, the reward of her merit is vast. Because she gave rise to a sincere heart amidst her suffering and distress, she has attained immeasurable blessings—the retribution corresponding to such merit."

Śakra Devānām Indra, though enjoying unrestrained luxury in the heavens, relinquished his noble and honored status to descend and plant roots of merit; the retribution he obtained is immeasurable. For this reason, the Tathāgata said that dāna (generosity) is foremost.
"The people of Jambudvīpa are foolish and pitiable; those who are like this are but few. You should widely proclaim the true words of the Tathāgata.

When the Buddha spoke these words, devas, nāgas, spirits, the fourfold assembly, and the community of bhikṣus performed great meritorious deeds and offered alms, vowing that their merit should extend to all sentient beings, so that all might obtain their desired fruits according to their aspirations.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the entire assembly was filled with joy; they bowed their heads in prostration and paid homage.
This concludes the *Mahākāśyapa Sūtra on Saving the Poor Mother*.
